name: Seed oil avoidance

card.summary: Cutting canola, soybean, sunflower and similar oils for skin and health; popular online, while nutrition reviews generally do not support the harm claims.
card.aka: Hateful eight, seed oil free, tallow and butter cooking
card.note: No trials were found testing seed oil avoidance for skin or looks; major reviews of dietary evidence do not support the harm claims.

quick.overview:
Seed oil avoidance means removing refined vegetable oils such as canola, soybean, sunflower, corn and safflower from the diet and cooking with fats like butter, tallow or olive oil. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a way to improve skin, inflammation and general health, often alongside carnivore or primal eating.

Nutrition reviews and health bodies generally report that these oils do not reliably raise inflammation and that replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat is associated with better cardiovascular markers. No clinical studies were found that test seed oil avoidance for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Proponents point to omega-6 linoleic acid (said to promote inflammation), a high omega-6 to omega-3 ratio, and industrial solvent extraction as reasons for harm. Researchers say trials do not show linoleic acid reliably raising inflammatory markers and that absolute intake, not the ratio, should guide advice.
quick.risks: Avoiding seed oils is not itself documented as harmful, but reviews note that shifting toward saturated fat could raise LDL cholesterol. Forum users also note it is hard to avoid oils in restaurants, and some posters acknowledge that the effect size is unclear.

lead: Seed oil avoidance is a dietary practice in which people exclude refined oils pressed or solvent-extracted from seeds, such as canola, soybean, sunflower, corn, cottonseed, safflower, grapeseed and rice bran, often called the 'hateful eight' in online discussion.[1] Adherents say the oils drive inflammation, skin problems and chronic disease; in looksmaxxing forums it is bundled with other 'clean' eating ideas.[2][3]

Reviews of human evidence report that linoleic acid, the main omega-6 fat in these oils, does not reliably raise inflammatory markers, and that replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat is linked to better cardiovascular risk markers.[1][4][5] A 2025 narrative review describes the campaign against seed oils as contrary to dietary guidelines and available human research.[4] No clinical studies were found testing seed oil avoidance for skin or facial appearance.

Butter, beef tallow, olive oil, coconut oil

paras: Seed oils are fats obtained from the seeds of plants and used for cooking, packaged foods and, in other forms, topical products.[6] Critics of the oils usually target eight refined oils, a grouping popularised by physician Cate Shanahan on a podcast in 2020.[1]
Practitioners avoid them in home cooking and restaurants, sometimes consulting lists of restaurants said to cook with butter or tallow.[7]

According to Wikipedia, a movement claiming that refined vegetable oils drive chronic disease circulated online from about 2018 and gained wide attention in 2020 after podcaster Joe Rogan interviewed carnivore-diet promoter Paul Saladino.[1] Wikipedia also records that opposition to seed oils later entered US political discussion, including statements by Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in 2024 and 2025.[1]
In looksmaxxing forums the topic appears in jokes and serious threads, including a satirical 'seed oils will ascend you' post and practical threads about which fast-food chains avoid them.[2][7]

Proponents argue that industrial processing with solvents such as hexane, high omega-6 linoleic acid content and a high omega-6 to omega-3 ratio promote inflammation and disease, and they extend this to skin and appearance.[1][2] Some forum members suggest taking krill oil to rebalance omega-3 when eating out; others reply that cooking at home with olive oil or butter is sufficient.[8]

A 2025 narrative review in Nutrition Reviews concluded that the human evidence does not support the claim that seed oils drive cardiometabolic disease and noted that saturated fat is linked to higher LDL cholesterol.[4] A 2025 systematic review examined seed-oil effects on lipid profile, inflammatory and oxidative markers and glycemic control in diabetic and dyslipidemic patients.[9]

A randomized trial in overweight and obese adults found no evidence of differing effects between sunflower and rapeseed oil on coronary artery disease and chronic kidney disease biomarkers.[10] A review of the omega-6 to omega-3 ratio in Missouri Medicine argued that a lower ratio may reduce autoimmune, asthma and allergy risk, a position cited by some proponents.[11]

Wikipedia reports that the World Cancer Research Fund and Cancer Council Australia have stated there is no evidence seed oils raise cancer risk, and that the US FDA considers consumer vegetable oils generally recognized as safe.[1]

Research on seed oils for skin mostly concerns topical use rather than dietary avoidance. A review of African plant oils in dermatology describes traditional topical uses, with potential benefits and adverse effects.[6] These findings do not address whether eating seed oils changes skin appearance.

No studies found testing seed oil avoidance for skin or appearance. Related human research on dietary seed oils examines cardiometabolic markers, including a randomized trial of sunflower versus rapeseed oil and systematic reviews of lipid and inflammatory outcomes.[9][10]

timeline.event: Procter & Gamble introduces cottonseed-based Crisco as a lard substitute.[1]
Canola oil receives US generally-recognized-as-safe status.[1]
Online movement claiming refined vegetable oils cause chronic disease begins to circulate.[1]
Joe Rogan interviews Paul Saladino; 'hateful eight' label popularised.[1]
Robert F. Kennedy Jr. blames seed oils for health problems when ending his presidential campaign.[1]

lore.intro: Seed oil avoidance appears on looksmax.org as a health and skin theory, a joke ('seed oils will ascend you'), and a practical question of how to eat out without them.[2][7][8]

claims.claim: Seed oils cause inflammation that harms skin and looks
claims.believers: Proponents say the omega-6 content of these oils promotes inflammation, and some forum members count them among things to avoid.[2]
claims.experts: Reviews report that linoleic acid does not reliably raise inflammatory markers, and no study has tested seed oil avoidance for skin appearance.[1][4]

claims.claim: A high omega-6 to omega-3 ratio is harmful
claims.believers: Users suggest supplementing krill oil to rebalance the ratio after eating seed-oil-cooked food.[8]
claims.experts: A Missouri Medicine review argues for a low ratio to reduce autoimmune, asthma and allergy risk, while Wikipedia cites a 2024 review that absolute intake, not ratio, should guide advice.[1][11]

claims.claim: Restaurant food is full of seed oils and should be avoided
claims.believers: Forum posters compile lists of chains that cook in butter, tallow or seed oils.[7]
claims.experts: Regulators regard consumer vegetable oils as generally recognized as safe, and no trial has tested restaurant avoidance for health or appearance.[1]

claims.claim: Replacing seed oils with saturated fat is healthier
claims.believers: Carnivore and primal diet advocates promote butter and tallow in place of vegetable oils.[1][7]
claims.experts: The 2025 review notes excess saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol and that guidelines recommend replacing it with unsaturated fat.[4]
